_readme: Copy library for the seven lifecycle emails. PostHog holds only whichever variant is currently live on each step - this file is the source of truth and its git history is the record of every decision the weekly loop has made. build_email.py turns an entry here into the exact payload workflows-patch-action-email expects; decide.py chooses which entry that should be; optimise.md is the runbook the scheduled job follows. Exactly one variant per step is 'champion' and at most one is 'testing'; two can never be live at once because PostHog has no split node, which is why the test is sequential - see the top of decide.py for what that costs.

_angles.utility: No persuasion. Tells them the one thing to do and gets out of the way.
_angles.question: Subject is a real question. Questions are the highest-opening subject format measured (~46%), and a reply is the cleanest engagement signal there is.
_angles.specific: Concrete number or outcome in the subject. Specific curiosity beats vague teasing by ~26%; vague teasing also wins opens and loses clicks.
_angles.empathy: Names the awkwardness out loud. Beats urgency on win-back - 'did we lose you' outperforms 'final notice'.
_angles.confession: Leads with something that went wrong on our side. The register that earned 29% replies on the old campaign.
_angles.peer: Speaks in another user's voice rather than the company's. Unlocks accounts that company-voice email cannot.
_angles.permission: Offers to stop emailing. Counter-intuitively strong on dormant lists and cleans the list either way.
_angles.research: Ask to buy their time, not their money. The offer is credits for an interview; the conversion that matters is a booked call, so the click is the result.

checkout_1.url_note:
Sends 15 minutes after the trigger. The CTA carries the PLAN, never a payment link.

Dodo checkout sessions expire after about 15 minutes, so no email can ship a working one: delivery plus the time before someone opens it routinely exceeds that, and an expired Dodo page is a dead end with an error rather than a way to pay. An earlier version templated event.properties.checkout_url into the button; it was reverted on 24 Aug for exactly this.

Instead the link is /app?action=upgrade&plan=<plan>, and app.html mints the session ON THE CLICK, from a browser already signed in (resolvePlanParam + proceedToCheckoutDirect). Nothing can expire, because nothing exists until they click. It is also why no account identifier travels in the URL: app.html reads ?token= into localStorage, so an identifying link would hand whoever opened it that account.

The Liquid handles both triggers, and both branches were verified with workflows-test-run:
  checkout_redirect_started -> plan_key   -> &plan=pro_monthly
  plan_selected             -> plan+billing -> &plan=Enterprise&billing=annual
resolvePlanParam accepts both shapes and returns null for anything else, so an unrecognised plan opens the pricing modal rather than guessing one the person never chose.

NOT applied to checkout_2 - it fires 3 days later and re-argues the offer rather than resuming a specific plan.

variants.subject: do not take my word on the data quality
variants.preheader: A five-minute test that settles it.
body: Every data company says its data is more accurate. You have no way to check that from an email, and neither would I.
So here is how to actually settle it, in about five minutes:

Take ten people you personally know — colleagues, past clients, people whose details you can verify. Run them through LinkFinder. Count how many come back right, how many come back empty, and how many come back wrong.

Empty is honest and cheap to work around. Wrong is the one that costs you, because a bad email hurts your sending reputation. That ratio is the only quality number that matters, and it is the one you can measure yourself in five minutes.
Do that test on us — you still have credits on your account.
after: Whatever you find, I would like to see it. Good or bad, reply with the numbers — if we are getting a category of person wrong I want to know which.

body: By this point in the sequence you are either using LinkFinder again or you have not yet found your reason to. So here is what people actually do with it — it is rarely what they signed up for.
Filling a CRM that went stale. A few thousand contacts with missing emails and titles, enriched in one pass.
Turning a conference list into an outreach list. Names and companies from an attendee PDF, out the other side as verified emails.
Enriching inbound signups. Someone fills in a form with a work email; you want their title and company size before sales calls them.
Finding who else is worth talking to. One good customer, then everyone at that company with a matching job title.
after: If your use case is not on that list, tell me what it is — the odd ones are usually the most interesting, and sometimes they turn into features.

variants.hypothesis: Offering to stop is counter-intuitively strong on dormant lists and cleans the list either way: a reply is engagement, an unsubscribe removes an address that was depressing every future metric. Ending a ten-email sequence any other way would be the wrong note - the whole point was to earn attention, not extract it.
variants.subject: should I stop emailing you?
variants.preheader: Genuine question, and either answer is fine.
body: This is the last email in this sequence, so it is a fair moment to ask directly: do you want to keep hearing from me?
You have had ten emails from me over three months. If none of them made you want to open LinkFinder again, that is a real answer and I would rather act on it than keep sending into a void.
If not: the unsubscribe link below works instantly, and there is no follow-up sequence waiting behind it.
If yes, but not yet: nothing to do. Your credits do not expire, the tasks stay claimable, and the account stays as it is. Come back whenever there is a list to work through.
If something was missing: reply and tell me what. Several of the things I described in these emails exist because someone replied to one like this.
after: Either way — thank you for reading this far. Most people do not.
